title: Layered Bob Styling Tutorial
metaDescription: How to style a layered bob at home for movement instead of a flat helmet shape — a round-brush blowout method that works on fine and medium hair.

steps.name: Prep towel-dried hair
steps.text: Apply heat protectant and a small amount of mousse to damp, towel-dried hair, focusing product at the roots for lift.

steps.name: Section top from bottom
steps.text: Clip the top half of the hair up and start blow-drying the bottom section first, working in small pieces.

steps.name: Round-brush each section
steps.text: Wrap small sections around the round brush and follow with the dryer nozzle pointed down the hair shaft, rolling the brush under at the ends for a slight inward curve.

steps.name: Work through the top layers
steps.text: Release the top section and repeat, angling the brush to lift the roots away from the scalp as you dry for volume at the crown.

steps.name: Set the layers
steps.text: Once fully dry, run a flat iron or curling wand lightly over the ends for extra shape, then finish with a light-hold spray.

tips.question: Why does a layered bob go flat by midday?
tips.answer: Skipping the root lift step during blow-drying is the most common cause — a bob with no volume built in at the crown falls flat as soon as the initial style relaxes, regardless of how the ends are curled.

tips.question: What round brush size works best for a bob length?
tips.answer: A medium barrel, roughly 1.5 inches, gives enough curve to shape the ends without being too large to maneuver through shorter layers.

tips.question: Can a layered bob be air-dried instead?
tips.answer: Yes, with a light mousse scrunched in and the ends tucked under with fingers while damp — it won't have as much volume at the root, but it holds shape reasonably well on wavy textures.

storyIntro: A layered bob is one of the most requested cuts precisely because it looks effortless in photos — but that soft, face-framing movement almost always comes from how it's styled, not just how it's cut.
The round-brush blowout technique is what builds the volume at the root and the slight inward curve at the ends that separates a "styled" bob from one that's just air-dried flat.
storyNote: Dry each section completely before moving to the next one — going back over a partially dry section with the round brush is what causes frizz and undoes the smoothness from the first pass.
